documents.title: HNSW Graph Construction
documents.text: HNSW builds a hierarchical navigable small-world graph for approximate nearest-neighbor search. Each inserted vector receives a randomly sampled maximum layer. New nodes connect to nearby candidates at each eligible layer, with bounded neighbor lists controlled by M. Upper layers provide long-range navigation while layer zero contains the densest connections. efConstruction controls the breadth of candidate exploration during insertion; increasing it can improve graph quality at additional build cost.

documents.title: HNSW Query Search
documents.text: An HNSW query begins at the entry point on the highest populated layer. Greedy search moves to closer neighbors while descending through upper layers. At layer zero, a best-first search explores a candidate set whose breadth is controlled by efSearch. A larger efSearch generally improves recall but increases query latency and memory traffic.

documents.title: Vector Persistence Format
documents.text: A persistent vector store must serialize identifiers, metadata, dimensions, and floating-point coordinates. A versioned file header allows the loader to reject incompatible formats. Length fields should be bounded before allocating memory. A safe save operation writes a temporary snapshot, flushes it, and only then replaces the previous database file.

documents.title: Atomic Snapshot Replacement
documents.text: Atomic persistence avoids leaving a partially written database after a crash. The application writes a complete new snapshot to a temporary file, checks write and flush results, and preserves the previous snapshot until the new file is ready. Recovery logic can validate the primary file and fall back to a known-good backup when necessary.

documents.title: Document Chunking Strategy
documents.text: Long documents are divided into smaller overlapping text chunks before embedding. Chunk size controls how much context each vector represents, while overlap reduces the chance that a fact split at a boundary loses its surrounding meaning. Chunking should preserve useful headings and metadata so retrieved passages can be traced back to their source document.

documents.title: Embedding Model Inference
documents.text: An embedding model maps text into a dense numerical vector so semantically related passages can be compared. The same model and preprocessing rules should be used for both indexed documents and incoming questions. Changing the embedding model or its dimensionality generally requires re-embedding the corpus and rebuilding the vector index.

documents.title: Cosine Similarity
documents.text: Cosine similarity compares the angle between two vectors rather than their raw magnitudes. Cosine distance is commonly computed as one minus cosine similarity. It is useful when vector direction represents semantic meaning and vector magnitude is not intended to dominate ranking. Implementations must handle zero-length vectors explicitly to avoid division by zero.

documents.title: Euclidean Distance
documents.text: Euclidean distance is the square root of the sum of squared coordinate differences between two vectors. It measures straight-line distance in the embedding space and is sensitive to vector magnitude. For a KD-Tree, the distance from a query to a splitting plane can provide a lower bound for deciding whether the opposite subtree may contain a closer point.

documents.title: Manhattan Distance
documents.text: Manhattan distance is the sum of absolute coordinate differences between two vectors. It measures movement along coordinate axes and is also called L1 distance. A KD-Tree can use the absolute difference on its split axis as a lower bound when deciding whether a far subtree can be skipped.

documents.title: KD-Tree Construction
documents.text: A KD-Tree recursively partitions points using one coordinate axis at each level. A common construction strategy selects a median point to keep the tree balanced, then cycles through dimensions for subsequent splits. Incremental insertion without rebalancing can create a skewed tree and degrade search toward linear time.

documents.title: KD-Tree High-Dimensional Limits
documents.text: KD-Tree pruning depends on geometric lower bounds from axis-aligned partitions. In high-dimensional spaces, points often become difficult to separate using a single coordinate, so many branches must be visited. This dimensionality effect can make KD-Tree queries approach brute-force cost for dense text embeddings.

documents.title: Brute-Force Nearest Neighbors
documents.text: Brute-force search computes the distance from the query to every stored vector, sorts or selects the best candidates, and returns the top K. It is exact for the selected distance function and is a useful ground-truth baseline for measuring approximate-neighbor recall. Its query cost grows linearly with the number of vectors and dimensions.

documents.title: ANN Recall Measurement
documents.text: Recall@K compares the approximate index's returned neighbors with the exact top-K neighbors from a ground-truth search. It is calculated as the number of overlapping result IDs divided by K, averaged over a query set when reporting aggregate recall. Recall should be measured alongside latency because faster search may return fewer exact neighbors.

documents.title: REST API Validation
documents.text: A REST API should validate required fields, data types, vector dimensions, and numeric values before modifying the database. Invalid requests should return clear client-error status codes and useful messages. Validation at the boundary prevents malformed vectors or missing metadata from reaching indexing and persistence code.

documents.title: Document Ingestion Endpoint
documents.text: A document ingestion route accepts a title and text, validates that both are present, splits the text into chunks, obtains embeddings, and stores each chunk with source metadata. The response should identify inserted records so clients can report success and later delete or inspect the stored content.

documents.title: Retrieval-Only API
documents.text: A retrieval-only endpoint embeds the user's question, searches the document index, and returns the top matching passages with their metadata. It does not invoke a text-generation model. Separating retrieval from answer generation makes it easier to debug search quality and measure retrieval metrics independently.

documents.title: RAG Answer Generation
documents.text: A RAG answer endpoint retrieves relevant document chunks and places their text into a prompt together with the user's question. A local language model generates a response grounded in the supplied context. The application should return both the answer and retrieved passages so users can inspect the evidence used by the model.

documents.title: Ollama Model Roles
documents.text: A local RAG system commonly uses one Ollama model for embeddings and another for text generation. The embedding model converts documents and questions into vectors; the generative model reads retrieved passages and writes an answer. Both models must be available before the complete RAG workflow can run.

documents.title: RAG Hit Rate and MRR
documents.text: Hit Rate@K measures the fraction of questions for which at least one relevant document appears in the top K results. Mean Reciprocal Rank averages the reciprocal of the first relevant result's rank, rewarding systems that place relevant evidence nearer the top. These metrics evaluate retrieval ordering rather than the factual correctness of generated answers.

documents.title: Context Precision
documents.text: Context Precision@K measures how much of the retrieved context is relevant to a query. A system can achieve a perfect hit rate while still returning several irrelevant chunks in the same top-K result list. Reporting both metrics distinguishes finding at least one correct source from keeping the overall retrieved context focused.

documents.title: Answer Keyword Coverage
documents.text: A simple answer keyword coverage metric checks whether selected expected terms appear in a generated response. It is inexpensive and deterministic, but it is only a diagnostic: correct paraphrases may omit exact terms, while an answer can include keywords without being factually correct. Human review or a validated semantic evaluator is needed for stronger answer-quality claims.

documents.title: Benchmark Reproducibility
documents.text: A useful performance benchmark fixes its dataset, query set, random seed, software build, and measurement procedure. It should report hardware and runtime conditions, repeat measurements, and summarize distributions such as median and tail latency rather than relying on one timing. Results should be compared under identical conditions.

documents.title: GitHub Actions Evaluation
documents.text: A continuous-integration workflow can compile the C++ benchmark, start the application and its dependencies, run API integration tests, and upload machine-readable reports as artifacts. Separating build, smoke-test, and evaluation jobs makes failures easier to identify. CI results prove that a defined test passed in that environment, not that every production workload is supported.

documents.title: Docker Compose Networking
documents.text: Docker Compose creates a network where services can reach each other by service name. A VectorForge container can therefore connect to the Ollama service using its Compose hostname instead of localhost. Named volumes can preserve database files and model caches when containers are recreated.

documents.title: Concurrency and Shared State
documents.text: A multithreaded vector database must protect shared indexes and persistence state from concurrent mutation. Mutexes can serialize critical sections, while read-write locks may allow concurrent readers when the data structure supports it. Lock scope should be kept small, and long-running model inference should not unnecessarily block unrelated search requests.

documents.title: API Security Boundaries
documents.text: A development REST API bound to loopback is not automatically safe to expose publicly. A public deployment should add authentication, authorization, transport encryption, request-size limits, rate limiting, and careful error handling. Secrets and internal model endpoints should not be exposed through client-controlled request fields.
